text: Stitching harness has two objects: strength and ornamentation.
Strength in stitching comes from using thread of the right size, making it up properly, using an awl that is neither too large nor too small, and drawing the work well together.
The thread sizes used by harness makers are Nos. 0, 10, 3, 12 and 5, with No. 5 the finest used.
Threads Nos. 5, 6 and 19 are of the same size but different colors: No. 5 is black, No. 6 is white and No. 19 is yellow.
The rule for choosing thread is to grade it according to the number of stitches to the inch.
No. 0 thread is the coarsest; it is made up with four strands and used where the stitches number eight or under to the inch.
No. 10 thread is a little lighter than No. 0; where the stitching is not more than ten nor less than eight to the inch, it is made up with three strands.
No. 3 thread is finer than No. 10 or No. 0 and is also used where the stitching runs from eight to ten to the inch, with four strands for all ordinary work.
For ten to sixteen stitches to the inch, No. 12 thread is used with four strands.
When the stitching is as fine as eighteen to the inch, No. 12 thread is used with only three strands.
For all work finer than eighteen stitches to the inch, No. 5 is the only thread used, made up with three or four strands according to the work.
The harness thread numbers refer to ball thread; skein thread differs little in size for the same numbers but looks finer because it is smoother.

For heavy work ball thread answers as well as skein thread, but while being twisted it should be well rubbed with the awl handle to remove irregularities; for fine, first-class work skein thread should be used.
White thread is preferred for heavy stitching by harness makers who have tested it, because it is stronger than colored thread.
In running off each strand of thread, examine it for hard, irregular spots; most small lumps are loose and can be removed without injury, and where they cannot, break the strand off and start anew.
Long threads are wanted for traces and other long straps to avoid starting a new thread in the body of the work, but ten to eleven feet is the greatest length that can be used to advantage.
Even a thread of ten to eleven feet is liable to be weakened by constant wear before it is used up.
To make a thread, untwist and pull apart the strand at the end, throw the center over a hook, and untwist and pull apart for the first strand; repeat until the required number of strands is obtained.

Untwisting a strand before parting it separates the fibres without breaking them and gives a smooth, tapered end; a strand that is broken off has an irregular end that is troublesome when threading needles or attaching bristles.
There are two opinions on waxing thread: some wax only after the strands are twisted together, while others do most of the waxing before twisting.

Examining used thread supports waxing before twisting: so little wax remains on the surface that it adds neither strength nor water resistance, while strands waxed before twisting keep all but the surface wax.
Fine threads may be waxed after twisting, but all heavy threads should be well waxed before twisting.
After the strands are broken off, rub them by giving one turn around the awl handle and rubbing back and forth, then apply the wax and twist up moderately firm.
A thread twisted too firmly will not take the wax well and wears away rapidly; a thread left too loose lets the strands open and show after the stitch is laid.
Shoemaker's black wax, the best wax for general use on thread, is made of equal parts of pitch and tallow.
Ordinary shoemaker's black wax is too hard for winter; the winter proportions are one pound of tallow to three quarters of a pound of pitch.
Black wax will not do for white or light-colored thread; a good wax for these is made of refined pitch and tallow, in proportions set by the hardness wanted.
Ordinary yellow and white wax are also used for light thread, but they are not as good as wax made of pitch.
The prick wheel helps greatly in keeping stitches of equal length, but irregularities still occur unless the workman handles his awl correctly.
Straight stitching was once avoided by leading manufacturers because it looked like machine work, but once machines could imitate any hand stitch the straight stitch became popular again.
Leading manufacturers lay all heavy stitches of ten or less to the inch at a moderate angle, using a diamond-shaped awl.
To keep angled stitches uniform, the awl is held so that a face of the angle is parallel with the top of the jaw of the stitching-horse, and part of the awl handle is flattened to match that angle.
If the stitching is sixteen or less to the inch the angle of the stitch is reduced, and all stitches of more than sixteen to the inch are laid straight.
Drawing harder on one thread than on the other produces irregular stitches.
A common fault of stitchers is tightening the thread in one motion as soon as it is short enough; whatever the length of the thread, the tightening up should always be a distinct motion.

For flat stitches the force applied to both threads should be equal; for a full stitch on the face side, the thread bearing against the under side should be drawn the tightest, but not enough to draw out the channeling.
Stitchers tend to draw the thread in the awl hand the tightest, and it takes practice to overcome this.

Where stitches show equally from both sides, enter the needles and, when the one on the left side is drawn nearly out, bring the loose thread forward, throw it over the needle, and tighten up as usual; the work then looks nearly as well on the reverse as on the right side.
The awl should be driven through at right angles with the face of the leather and held so that it always enters in the same position.
Stitches should never be buried into the leather, because this tends to weaken the work, not strengthen it.
